Offscouring
OFF-skow-ring
noun
From off + scouring — that which is scoured off in cleaning: the scrapings, the filth wiped from a vessel and thrown away. It renders the Greek peripsema, the dirt rubbed off all around, and the Hebrew of Lamentations for refuse and sweepings.

Biblical Definition

Offscouring is what is scraped off and thrown out — the scourings of a pot, the filth wiped from a dish, the refuse no one keeps. It is the lowest word a man can use of himself, and Paul uses it of the apostles. Cataloguing what the ministry had cost them — hunger, thirst, nakedness, buffeting, homelessness, labour with their own hands — he ends: “Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day” (1Co 4:13). He had already said God had set forth the apostles last, “as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men” (1Co 4:9). Note the sting in the context: he wrote it to a church that thought itself full, rich, reigning as kings — wise, strong, honourable in its own eyes — while the men who brought them the gospel were the world’s garbage. Jeremiah had wept the same word over Zion: “Thou hast made us as the offscouring and refuse in the midst of the people” (Lam 3:45). And the word has a Master. Christ was despised and rejected, cast out of the city as a thing unclean, and so the writer to the Hebrews calls the church after Him: “Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13). Outside the camp is where the ashes were carried and the refuse burned; it is also where the Lord of glory hung. The offscouring of all things is not an accident of the apostolic age. It is the uniform.

Webster 1828 Definition

That which is scoured off; the scrapings, refuse, or filth of a thing — used by Paul of the apostles themselves.

OFFSCOURING, that which is scoured off; refuse; the filth wiped away and cast out.

From off and scour; it renders the Greek peripsema, dirt rubbed off all around.

It is the meanest thing a man can be called, and Paul owns it (1Co 4:13).

Jeremiah laments that Zion was made the offscouring in the midst of the people (Lam 3:45).

The apostles were a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men (1Co 4:9).

Key Scripture

1Co 4:13 — "Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day."

Lam 3:45 — "Thou hast made us as the offscouring and refuse in the midst of the people."

1Co 4:9 — "For I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men."

Heb 13:13 — "Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach."

Modern Corruption

Paul’s word for the apostles: the world’s garbage. It stands squarely against a religion of platforms, brands, and prosperity.

expand to see more

The live corruption is the exact inversion of this word by the prosperity-and-platform religion of our day. Paul says the apostles were set forth last, appointed to death, a spectacle to the world, the filth of it, the offscouring of all things — and he says it in deliberate contrast to a Corinthian church that was full, rich, and reigning as kings without them. That contrast has been resolved the wrong way. The modern teacher measures his calling by his following, his book sales, his jet, his brand; he preaches a Christ who will make you full, rich, and reigning now; and he holds up the very things Paul held up as evidence that Corinth had misunderstood the gospel. If the apostolic ministry looked like offscouring and the modern ministry looks like Corinth, it is not the apostles who need explaining.

The principle to recover is that shame borne for Christ is the pattern, not the exception. Christ was led outside the city as an unclean thing, to the place where the refuse was burned, and the writer to the Hebrews draws the only conclusion: let us go forth therefore unto Him without the camp, bearing His reproach. The camp has the crowds, the honour, and the applause; the Lord is outside it. A servant is not greater than his master, and the disciple who is never counted the offscouring of anything should ask whether he has followed his Lord out of the gate at all. This is no counsel of despair — being defamed, Paul says, we intreat; he answered slander with entreaty and reproach with the gospel. But it is the sober arithmetic of discipleship: the men who turned the world upside down were, in the world’s ledger, its garbage, and they reckoned the trade a bargain.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means that which is scoured off — scrapings, refuse, the filth cast out.

expand to see more

Offscouring — from off + scouring, what is scraped away.

It renders the Greek peripsema, the dirt rubbed off all around a vessel.

It names the refuse of the world, the thing no one keeps.

Paul calls the apostles the offscouring of all things (1Co 4:13).

Zion was made the offscouring in the midst of the people (Lam 3:45).

Usage

"We are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things — the apostles’ uniform."

"Corinth reigned as kings while the men who brought them Christ were counted the world’s refuse."

"Christ was cast without the camp: go forth unto Him there, bearing His reproach."
